newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to vote in close, high-stakes election.
newsitem.headline: France to vote in close, high-stakes election.

text.p: France votes on Sunday in the first round of a parliamentary election that could give President Jacques Chirac a like-minded centre-right majority for five years or force him to share power with a leftwing government.

Chirac called the May 25/June 1 election 10 months ahead of schedule, saying he needed a "new elan" to lead France into a single European currency and press ahead with gradual market economic reforms.
Seeking to catch the opposition by surprise, he deliberately set a short campaign, punctuated by three long public holiday weekends and a busy sports and diplomatic calendar.

But opinion polls published before last weekend's legal blackout suggested the combined left had drawn almost level with the ruling coalition in voting intentions, although all projected a reduced centre-right majority of seats.

Rumours of secret polls showing the race tightening still further made the Paris Bourse jittery on Thursday, sending shares down one percent in early trading. But the franc was steady against the German mark.

Voters face a sharp choice of economic policies, although the centre-right is careful not to propose the kind of radical deregulation of the heavily state-dominated society which the U.S. Republicans and British Conservatives implemented.

The Socialist and Communist opposition promises to attack France's record 12.8 percent unemployment -- the highest rate among the Group of Seven major industrial powers -- by creating 700,000 youth jobs, half of them in the public sector, and reducing the work week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay.

The centre-right coalition led by Prime Minister Alain Juppe promises a public spending freeze, tax cuts, an accelerated privatisation programme and a gradual reduction in the civil service to give more scope for private initiative.

Although French voters do not choose the prime minister, which is the sole prerogative of the president, the campaign has been highly personalised between Juppe and Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin, who is widely regarded as having run a good race.

The left has hammered home the message that the 38 million voters should cast their ballots against "five more years of Juppe", blaming the unpopular premier for unemployment, high taxes and curbs on the generous welfare state.
Sources close to Chirac say the president would like to reappoint Juppe and believes there is another year's hard work to be done to prepare for European economic and monetary union.

But other conservative politicians say privately -- and some publicly -- that Juppe is a liability and should be dumped if the centre-right wins a very narrow victory, losing more than 150 of its 464 seats in the 577-member National Assembly.
Polls show voters would prefer Eurosceptical National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, a socially-minded Gaullist, or ex-premier Edouard Balladur as prime minister.

Chirac has sought to sway the campaign and shield Juppe by intervening to attack the Socialists' record and warning voters that France's voice in Europe would be weakened by another period of left-right power-sharing, known as "cohabitation".

The conservatives have played up differences within the left on the single European currency, which the Socialists support conditionally but the Communists oppose, as well as on wages and privatisations.

After initially saying the left would halt current plans to privatise France Telecom and defence firm Thomson-CSF, Jospin appeared to shift ground this week, saying he would consult the telephone company's staff. Economists said the Socialists would need the money from the planned sale of a minority stake. Juppe has now raised the prospect of faster privatisation if the right won, telling business daily Les Echos the government might privatise Air France and state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais this year in addition to Thomson-CSF and France Telecom.

The extreme-right National Front seems set to poll about 15 percent of the vote, benefiting from conservative voters angry at Chirac and Juppe. But it is forecast to win only two or three seats, if any, because of the two-round voting system.
How National Front voters switch on the runoff in seats where their candidate fails to qualify for the second round could shape the outcome of the election, pollsters say.
Relations between the Socialists and Communists have been touchy. They signed a joint election declaration which skirted their differences on the single European currency.
Since then Jospin has said that, as the largest force on the left, the Socialists would set the line on the issue, prompting Communist leader Robert Hue to accuse him of attempts to impose hegemony.
